section: 1.  Identify the most-recent date tag among saved CSVs
grain_in: one file on disk in results/ matching <base_name>_YYYY-MM-DD.csv
grain_out: one row per base name (nine requested bases, fewer if files are absent)
units_out: file paths, one selected path per base
operation: Lists files in results/ whose name matches one of nine hard-coded base names followed by an ISO date, parses base and date out of the filename, drops bases not in the requested set, then sorts by base, descending date, descending filename and keeps the first row per base, so each base is represented by whichever file carries the newest date string. The tibble build and the filter are absorbed because they only parse and restrict the file list that the slice then reduces; the warning block is absorbed because it only reports which bases produced no file and does not stop the run.
settings: Nine base names listed explicitly, including both beta_bray_pairs_monthly and beta_bray_bay_period_season; regex requires the suffix _YYYY-MM-DD.csv; recency is taken from the date in the filename, not from file contents or modification time; tie within a date broken by descending fname; slice_head(n = 1) per base; results_dir is script_dir/results.
na_behavior: A filename matching the regex whose date fails as.Date yields NA in date; dplyr::arrange sorts NA last even under desc(), so such a file is chosen only when it is the only candidate for its base. A base with no matching file produces a warning only: the run continues, the object is never created, and the failure surfaces later as an object-not-found error at the aliasing step. A missing results/ directory returns an empty listing, which is indistinguishable here from a directory whose filenames are all misspelled.

section: 2. Read each latest file into a named list
grain_in: one row per base (a file path)
grain_out: one data frame per base; for the tables used downstream, one row per major_area x period x season (beta_bray is one row per major_area x season x year2; beta_bray_pairs_monthly is one row per site pair per month)
units_out: mixed: species counts and Shannon diversity, a synchrony index in [0,1], invariability ratios, a portfolio ratio, Bray-Curtis dissimilarities
operation: Reads each selected CSV with readr::read_csv, deframes the result into a named list, pushes that list into the global environment, aliases the long names to short ones, and deletes every other object. The read is the node; the deframe, list2env and the aliases are absorbed because they only carry the tables forward under new names. The aliasing does embed one choice that is not a pure rename: beta_bray is bound to beta_bray_bay_period_season while beta_bray_pairs_monthly is bound to beta_bray_montn, so the two Bray tables are assigned different roles here. Column meanings are taken from the CSVs and cannot be checked from this script; the block comment for com_inv says its stability column is community_invariability, which the downstream transmute does not use.
settings: show_col_types = FALSE, so column types are guessed by readr defaults and never reported; keep_objs retains alpha_div, gamma_div, beta_div, beta_bray, synchrony, portfolio, pop_inv, com_inv, P, script_dir, beta_bray_montn; everything else in the environment is removed.
na_behavior: read_csv turns empty fields and the default NA strings into NA silently, and a stray token in a numeric column makes the whole column character without an error here. If a base was missing at the previous node the alias line stops the script with an object-not-found error, so a missing input and a corrupt input fail in different ways. Nothing checks that the tables share the same set of major_area, period and season values.

grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season, in three separate tables (community invariability, synchrony, alpha diversity)
grain_out: one row per major_area x period x season carrying community invariability, synchrony and alpha diversity side by side
units_in: invariability ratio; synchrony index in [0,1]; richness in species and Shannon diversity
operation: Left joins synchrony and then alpha_div onto com_inv on major_area, period and season, so com_inv sets the row set and any synchrony or diversity record without a matching com_inv row is dropped without notice. The region also contains eps, a constant used only by the following transform; it is recorded here because it sits above the pipeline and belongs to no earlier node. Whether com_inv is the right anchor table, and whether gamma_div and beta_div were meant to enter the model, cannot be settled from the code.
settings: left_join rather than inner_join; keys major_area, period, season in that order; com_inv is the left table; period is carried through the join but never enters any model.
na_behavior: A com_inv row with no synchrony match gets NA phi, and one with no alpha match gets NA richness and shannon. These become non-finite after the transform and are removed by the finite filter, so a failed join, a genuinely missing value in the source CSV, and a zero synchrony all leave the analysis in the same way and are not distinguishable afterwards. Duplicate keys on either right-hand table would multiply rows silently; nothing checks for that.

grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one row per major_area x period x season, restricted to the three keys and five analysis variables
units_in: synchrony index in [0,1]; invariability ratio; species count; Shannon diversity
units_out: natural log of a synchrony index; base-10 log of an invariability ratio; species count; Shannon diversity
operation: Keeps major_area, season, period and phi, and builds log_phi as the natural log of phi floored at eps and log_IC as the base-10 log of I_C, dropping every other column. Two things worth flagging: the two logs use different bases, natural for phi and base 10 for I_C, which matters when their coefficients are multiplied later; and the line creating I_C is commented out (#I_C = community_invariability,) while the transmute still refers to I_C, so the code requires a column literally named I_C in com_inv even though the block comment above says that table's stability column is community_invariability. Code and comments disagree here and the script cannot settle which name the CSV actually carries.
settings: eps = 1e-6 applied through pmax(phi, eps) before logging; log() for phi, log10() for I_C; phi kept alongside log_phi; all other columns from the three source tables discarded.
na_behavior: phi = NA gives pmax(NA, eps) = NA and so log_phi = NA. phi = 0 becomes log(1e-6) = -13.8, which is indistinguishable from a genuine phi of 1e-6, and any negative phi is silently raised to eps rather than flagged. I_C = 0 gives -Inf and I_C < 0 gives NaN. NA, -Inf and NaN all collapse to the same fate at the next filter, so a missing record, a zero, and a negative value cannot be told apart downstream.

grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season, including rows with missing or non-finite analysis variables
grain_out: one row per major_area x period x season for which all four analysis variables are finite; this is the population every model below describes
units_in: log synchrony, log10 invariability, species count, Shannon diversity
units_out: same, on the retained rows only
operation: Drops every row where log_phi, log_IC, richness or shannon is not finite, which is the step that fixes which area-period-season combinations the SEMs describe, then converts major_area and season to factors. The factor conversion is absorbed because it is a type change needed by lme's grouping, not a change of meaning. Nothing reports how many rows the filter removes or which areas or seasons lose coverage.
settings: is.finite applied to four columns and combined with AND; rows removed rather than flagged; no row count, no before-and-after comparison, no minimum-coverage rule per major_area or season.
na_behavior: is.finite is FALSE for NA, NaN, Inf and -Inf alike, so failures from four different causes (no match in the join, a missing value in the source CSV, phi at or below zero, I_C at or below zero) are removed by the same test and leave no trace. If the filter removes most rows for one major_area, the random-effects grouping later rests on very few observations for that level, and nothing in the script would show it.

grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one fitted mixed model (the diversity to synchrony path)
units_out: slope in log synchrony units per species, plus variance components
operation: Fits log_phi on richness by REML with random intercepts supplied as a list of two grouping factors. In nlme, random = list(major_area = ~1, season = ~1) specifies nested grouping, that is season within major_area, not crossed random effects; if seasons are the same labels repeated across areas, which the data description implies, the fitted structure is not the crossed design the setup comment suggests.
settings: REML; na.action = na.omit; random intercepts only, no random slopes; grouping list order major_area then season, which sets the nesting; period is not in the model as a fixed or random term, so repeated periods within an area and season are treated as independent.
na_behavior: na.omit silently drops any row with NA in a model variable, but the previous filter has already removed those, so this should not fire; if it did, this model would be fitted on a different row set from the companion model and the SEM would combine fits over different data without warning. Convergence failure raises an error and stops the script rather than returning a missing estimate.

grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one fitted mixed model (the direct richness path and the synchrony path to stability)
units_in: log10 invariability; richness in species; log synchrony
units_out: slopes in log10 invariability per species and per unit log synchrony, plus variance components
operation: Fits log_IC on richness and log_phi by REML with the same random structure, giving the direct effect of richness on stability while log_phi is held fixed and the effect of synchrony on stability. Richness enters both this model and the synchrony model, so the two paths are estimated from the same predictor and are not independent.
settings: REML; na.action = na.omit; random intercepts for major_area and season supplied as a nested list, as in the companion model; no interaction between richness and log_phi; period absent.
na_behavior: Same as the companion model: na.omit removes incomplete rows silently, and a fit that fails to converge stops the script rather than yielding a missing coefficient.

grain_out: one row per response-predictor path (coefficient tables), one row per response (R squared), one test statistic (Fisher's C)
units_in: model coefficients in log units per predictor unit
units_out: raw coefficients in the models' own units; standardized coefficients in standard deviation units; marginal and conditional R squared; a chi-square style statistic with df and p
operation: Assembles the two lme fits into a piecewise SEM and pulls out raw coefficients, standardized coefficients, R squared and the directed separation test. The four extraction lines are absorbed because each only reads the fitted object without changing what a coefficient means, except that standardize = scale changes the units of the estimates that the confidence intervals below are built on.
settings: psem given data = df_sem explicitly; standardize = "none" for the raw table and standardize = "scale" for the standardized table; the implied model has richness as an exogenous predictor of both log_phi and log_IC, which leaves few or no independence claims for Fisher's C to test.
na_behavior: With no missing paths there may be no independence claims, in which case fisherC returns a degenerate result (zero degrees of freedom) rather than an error, and the printed p-value should not be read as evidence of fit. rsquared can return NA for a component whose variance components are degenerate. Standardization by scale is undefined for a predictor with zero variance, which would surface as NA in the standardized table only.

grain_out: one row per path, reduced to response, predictor and a formatted string
units_in: standardized coefficient and its standard error, in standard deviation units
units_out: a character string holding a point estimate, a 95 percent interval and a standard error
operation: Computes Wald 95 percent confidence limits as the standardized estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors and pastes estimate, limits and standard error into one reporting string, then keeps only response, predictor and that string. The as_tibble call is absorbed because it only repairs an empty column name. Note the interval is built on the standardized estimates while the p-values printed alongside come from the raw table, and the numeric limits are discarded once formatted, so nothing downstream can recompute them.
settings: Normal quantile 1.96 rather than the t quantile with the degrees of freedom that coefs already reports, so the intervals are slightly narrow for the sample sizes involved; applied to the standardized (scale) coefficients, not the raw ones; three decimal places; .name_repair = "unique".
na_behavior: If Std.Error is NA the limits are NA and sprintf prints the string NA rather than failing, so a path that could not be estimated and a path whose standard error was dropped by standardization look identical in the reported table. The result is printed but never written to disk.

grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one fitted mixed model (the Shannon to synchrony path)
units_in: log synchrony; Shannon diversity (effective species at q = 1)
units_out: slope in log synchrony units per unit Shannon, plus variance components
operation: Same specification as the richness synchrony model with shannon substituted for richness, so it is a separate node because the predictor being checked differs. The two SEMs are fitted on the same rows and are not independent tests of the same hypothesis; nothing in the script adjusts for running both.
settings: REML; na.action = na.omit; random = list(major_area = ~1, season = ~1), which nlme reads as season nested within major_area; period absent.
na_behavior: As in the richness model: na.omit drops incomplete rows silently and a non-converging fit stops the script rather than returning a missing estimate.

grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one fitted mixed model (direct Shannon path and synchrony path to stability)
units_in: log10 invariability; Shannon diversity; log synchrony
units_out: slopes in log10 invariability per unit Shannon and per unit log synchrony, plus variance components
operation: Fits stability on Shannon diversity and log synchrony with the same random structure, giving the Shannon counterpart of the richness stability model.
settings: REML; na.action = na.omit; nested random intercepts as above; no interaction term; period absent.
na_behavior: As in the richness counterpart: rows with NA are dropped silently by na.omit, and failure to converge is an error rather than a missing value.

grain_out: one row per response-predictor path, one row per response for R squared, one Fisher's C statistic
units_in: model coefficients in log units per predictor unit
units_out: raw coefficients; standardized coefficients in standard deviation units; R squared; a test statistic with df and p
operation: Same assembly and extraction as the richness SEM, applied to the Shannon component models. Separate node because the inputs differ.
settings: psem with data = df_sem; standardize = "none" and standardize = "scale"; same saturated path structure, so the directed separation test has little or nothing to test.
na_behavior: As in the richness SEM: a saturated model yields a degenerate Fisher's C rather than an error, and rsquared may return NA for a degenerate variance component.

grain_out: one row per path, reduced to response, predictor and a formatted string
units_in: standardized coefficient and standard error in standard deviation units
units_out: a character string holding a point estimate, a 95 percent interval and a standard error
operation: Identical arithmetic to the richness confidence intervals, applied to the Shannon standardized coefficients; a separate node because the input table differs.
settings: Normal quantile 1.96 rather than a t quantile; standardized coefficients; three decimals; numeric limits discarded after formatting.
na_behavior: An NA standard error produces the literal string NA in the report, so an unestimable path is not distinguishable from a formatting failure. Printed only, never saved.

start_anchor: fig_logphi_rich <- ggplot(df_sem, aes(x = richness, y = log_phi)) +
end_context: fig_logphi_rich <- ggplot(df_sem, aes(x = richness, y = log_phi)) +
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season
grain_out: one figure: one point per row plus one fitted line and band
units_out: plotted values in the same units, plus an ordinary least squares slope and a 95 percent confidence band
operation: Plots log synchrony against richness with a straight line fitted by geom_smooth(method = "lm"). This is a second, different model of the same relationship: the line ignores the major_area and season random effects that the SEM component model uses, so the line drawn on the figure is not the path estimated in the text and the two can disagree in slope and in significance.
settings: method = "lm", se = TRUE so the band is a pointwise 95 percent confidence interval for the mean; point alpha 0.5; line width 1, black; theme_minimal; axes labelled Richness (q = 0) and log(phi).
na_behavior: ggplot would drop non-finite rows with a warning, but the input has already been filtered, so no rows should be lost here; if the filter upstream were removed, the figure and the models could silently describe different row sets.

start_anchor: fig_logphi_shan <- ggplot(df_sem, aes(x = shannon, y = log_phi)) +
grain_in: one row per major_area x period x season, plus the richness panel
grain_out: one two-panel figure and one TIFF file on disk
units_out: plotted values, an ordinary least squares slope and band per panel, and an image file
operation: Builds the Shannon panel with the same ordinary least squares smoother, then stacks the richness panel above it with patchwork, tags them a and b, and writes the result to results/fig_3_Synchrony_both.tif. The tag theme, the patchwork assembly, the redefinition of results_dir and the ggsave call are absorbed because they only carry the panels to disk; results_dir has to be rebuilt here because the earlier rm removed it. As with the richness panel, the plotted line is a fixed-effects only fit and does not correspond to the mixed model reported in the tables.
settings: method = "lm", se = TRUE; vertical stacking with the richness panel first; width 8.5 cm, height 12 cm, 600 dpi, TIFF with LZW compression; fixed output name fig_3_Synchrony_both.tif.
na_behavior: ggsave overwrites an existing file of the same name without warning and fails with an error if results/ does not exist, so a run that produced no figure and a run that overwrote yesterday's figure leave the same trace, namely a single file with the current timestamp.

grain_in: one row per response-predictor path in a raw coefficient table
grain_out: one scalar per call: the indirect effect of a diversity term on stability through synchrony
units_in: log synchrony per unit diversity; log10 invariability per unit log synchrony
units_out: log10 invariability per unit diversity, carried through a natural-log intermediate
operation: Defines the product of two raw path coefficients: the diversity to log_phi slope and the log_phi to log_IC slope. Because log_phi is a natural log and log_IC is a base-10 log, the intermediate cancels only if the same log_phi scale is used in both models, which it is here, but the resulting quantity is a base-10 log change in stability per unit diversity and should not be compared directly with the standardized coefficients reported above. The function computes no standard error, so the product is a point estimate with no uncertainty attached.
settings: standardize = "none", so the product is on the raw scale; paths selected by exact string match on Response and Predictor, with div_term supplied by the caller and the mediator fixed as log_phi.
na_behavior: If the string match finds no row, a or b is numeric(0) and the product is numeric(0) rather than NA, so a mislabelled predictor returns an empty value instead of an error and prints as nothing inside the message. If more than one row matched, the function would return a vector rather than a scalar. There is no check that either path was actually estimated.

grain_in: one row per path in the richness SEM raw coefficient table
units_in: log synchrony per species; log10 invariability per unit log synchrony
units_out: log10 invariability per species, through synchrony
operation: Calls the function on the richness SEM with the predictor label richness. A separate node from the definition because what is passed in is what is being checked: the label must match the Predictor string that coefs produces for this model.
settings: div_term = "richness"; result printed only when P == 1 and rounded to four decimals; never written to disk.
na_behavior: A label that does not match returns numeric(0), which round() passes through and message() prints as nothing, so a silent mismatch looks like an empty slot in the printed line rather than an error.

grain_in: one row per path in the Shannon SEM raw coefficient table
units_in: log synchrony per unit Shannon; log10 invariability per unit log synchrony
units_out: log10 invariability per unit Shannon, through synchrony
operation: Calls the same function on the Shannon SEM with the predictor label shannon; a separate node because the inputs differ from the richness call.
settings: div_term = "shannon"; printed only when P == 1, rounded to four decimals; never saved.
na_behavior: Same as the richness call: a label mismatch yields numeric(0) and prints as an empty value rather than raising an error.
